sources.news_title: SUPREME COURT SMACKDOWN: Justices Clear Way for Trump's Big Bend Border Wall in 8-1 Ruling
sources.text:
The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume building a border wall in West Texas' Big Bend Sector, staying a federal judge's injunction that had temporarily halted construction while a lawsuit proceeds.
The unsigned decision, issued by a divided court, found that the federal district judge in El Paso who issued the injunction last month had no authority to do so and that the administration was "extremely likely to prevail" on that point, according to NBC News. The court's ruling was 8-1, a lopsided margin that Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival highlighted in a post on X, writing: "When we filed in the Supreme Court, I called the district court's order halting wall construction 'as unprecedented as it is flawed.' We just won 8-1."
The lawsuit was brought by a coalition of environmental groups and local residents, including the Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church, and Danny Miller, a river guide who owns property in the area. They claim the Department of Homeland Security violated constitutional provisions by proceeding without congressional authorization and bypassing environmental regulations.
The Big Bend Sector spans more than 500 miles—roughly a quarter of the entire U.S.-Mexico border—though it accounted for just 1.3% of all border apprehensions in 2025, Reuters reported. Most of the proposed construction will take place on privately owned land, according to administration officials. A 17-mile barrier is slated for Big Bend National Park, though officials noted it will not feature the 30-foot steel pedestrian fencing planned elsewhere.
Administration officials have argued the wall is vital to stopping cartel operations active south of the border and curbing the smuggling of large quantities of illicit drugs into the United States. The government says 89,000 people have been detained trying to enter the country through the region in recent years, according to NBC News.
The legal dispute focuses on three waivers issued by then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in February and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, in May and July that allowed the government to evade environmental and conservation laws, the Washington Post reported.
Laiken Jordahl, a lawyer for the Center for Biological Diversity, blasted the ruling in a statement: "This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal."
The fight is not over. The environmental groups' lawsuit continues in the lower courts, and Monday's action merely lifts the injunction while litigation proceeds. The New York Times reported that the administration had asked the court to permit construction in areas including Big Bend National Park.
For Texans living and working along the border, the practical effect is immediate: construction equipment can move back in, and the administration can restart a project it argues is central to national security. Critics, including the plaintiffs in the suit, say the work will scar fragile desert habitat and national park land.
The decision arrives as the Trump administration presses ahead on multiple fronts—mass deportation, border wall completion, and a broader dismantling of what it calls the administrative state. Monday's ruling signals the high court is inclined to give the executive branch wide latitude on border security, at least for now.
Our Take
Eight to one. Let that sink in.
For months, radical environmental groups and their allies in the lower courts have done everything in their power to stop President Trump from finishing the wall—the same wall Congress funded, the same wall the American people voted for. One district judge in El Paso thought he could override the Commander-in-Chief on border security. The Supreme Court just told him he was wrong. Badly wrong.
This is what happens when you let activist judges run the show: cartels operate freely, drugs pour across the border, and the men and women of Border Patrol are left watching from the sidelines. Big Bend may only account for 1.3% of apprehensions, but that's not the point. The point is that every mile of open border is an invitation to human traffickers, fentanyl smugglers, and gang members who know exactly where the gaps are.
Notice the Left's reaction. No concern for the 89,000 people detained in that region. No concern for the Texas landowners whose property is being used as a smuggling corridor. Just outrage over desert habitat and canyon walls. Their priorities are clear—and they aren't yours.
The fight isn't over. The lawsuit continues, and the usual suspects will keep trying to tie this up in court. But Monday's ruling is a reminder: the Constitution put border security in the hands of the executive branch, not a single federal judge with an agenda.
Patriots, this is what winning looks like. The wall is going up. The only question now is how fast.

EXCLUSIVE: Trump Scores Major Supreme Court Victory as Justices Greenlight Border Wall Construction Despite Legal Battle
Nov. 9 2026, Published 8:26 p.m. ET
President Donald Trump has secured a significant Supreme Court victory in his administration's push to expand construction along the U.S.-Mexico border, after the nation's highest court intervened in a legal battle over a controversial Texas border wall project, RadarOnline.com can exclusively reveal.
According to Supreme Court documents reviewed by Radar the justices issued an emergency order on November 9 allowing the Trump administration to resume border barrier construction in Texas's Big Bend Sector, temporarily suspending a lower court ruling that had blocked the project.
The decision marks a significant development in the administration's ongoing efforts to accelerate border security construction despite legal challenges involving environmental protections and federal authority.
Supreme Court Intervenes in Border Wall Battle
The dispute, Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church, centers on the Department of Homeland Security's authority to bypass certain federal legal requirements when constructing barriers along the southern border.
Under Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, the Homeland Security secretary possesses broad authority to construct barriers and roads intended to deter unlawful border crossings.
The statute also allows the secretary to waive certain legal requirements deemed necessary to expedite construction.
Earlier this year, federal officials invoked that authority to advance construction in the Big Bend Sector, a region along the U.S.-Mexico border.
However, opponents challenged the project, raising concerns about the administration's use of waiver powers and the potential impact on protected environmental areas.
Trump Administration Secures Emergency Relief
The administration subsequently sought emergency intervention from the Supreme Court after a lower court blocked construction.
In its November 9 order, the Supreme Court granted relief allowing the administration to proceed while the underlying litigation continues.
The ruling effectively pauses the lower court's restriction, giving federal officials an opportunity to move forward with the disputed construction project.
However, the order does not represent a final determination that every aspect of the administration's border wall initiative complies with federal law.
Instead, the legal battle remains ongoing as the courts continue examining the scope of the federal government's authority.
Justice Jackson Breaks With Court
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented from the Supreme Court's decision, highlighting disagreement over the emergency intervention.
Her dissent comes as the administration continues to defend its interpretation of federal immigration laws and the extraordinary powers granted to Homeland Security officials.
The case raises broader questions about the extent to which federal agencies can bypass environmental safeguards when pursuing national border security objectives.
Border Construction Fight Far From Over
For Trump, the order removes an immediate legal obstacle to construction in the disputed Texas region.
For opponents, the underlying litigation remains an avenue to challenge the administration's actions.
The Supreme Court's intervention underscores the continuing legal conflict surrounding border enforcement, executive authority and environmental protections.
Although construction can resume under the emergency order, the ultimate resolution of the lawsuit remains unsettled.

sources.news_title: US Supreme Court allows border wall in Big Bend National Park to proceed
sources.text:
US Supreme Court allows border wall in Big Bend National Park to proceed
A lawsuit had sought to block border wall construction in the Big Bend National Park by targeting the waivers that sidestep environmental protections.
The United States Supreme Court has allowed President Donald Trump’s administration to build a border wall through a remote section of Big Bend National Park in West Texas.
In its decision on Monday, the court granted the government’s emergency request to lift a lower court’s injunction that had paused construction while the matter was litigated.
The injunction, it said, “impedes the Government from advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity”.
The border wall has long been a signature part of Trump’s platform to restrict immigration into the US.
During his first successful bid for the presidency in 2016, for instance, he rallied supporters with chants of “Build the wall!”
But the push to expand the border barrier through the popular national park has met pushback from conservationists, local officials and some members of Trump’s own Republican Party.
Big Bend National Park includes mountain ranges and desert that serve as a home to endangered species like the Mexican long-nosed bat.
Opponents say the plan to build the wall through the park would disrupt the ecologically and culturally significant landscape.
The Trump administration, however, has depicted the project as an urgent priority for national security and immigration control. It has described the Big Bend area as an artery for irregular border crossings and drug trafficking.
US District Judge Kathleen Cardone blocked the construction in October, noting that while the Big Bend sector makes up more than 25 percent of the US-Mexico border, it accounts for only 0.3 to 2.2 percent of migrant apprehensions.
“Therefore, if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire US-Mexico border,” Cardone wrote.
The Supreme Court, however, said the government was “exceedingly likely to prevail” on its argument that Cardone lacked jurisdiction under the 1996 Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act, which limits the ability of lower courts to rule on border barriers.
Under that law, district courts can only hear claims alleging a violation of the US Constitution. The Supreme Court found that the challengers’ claim did not qualify, writing that “there is no such thing as a ‘constitutional’ major-questions claim”.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to indicate she would have denied the government’s request. She did not explain her reasoning.
The Center for Biological Diversity was among the plaintiffs who brought the lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security, along with Friends of the Ruidosa Church and a local river guide and landowner.
The lawsuit challenged waivers used by the agency to fast-track border construction and sidestep environmental and conservation laws.
Without those waivers, plaintiffs said that construction would have to comply with laws such as the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act to alter the landscape in “one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States”.

sources.news_title: SCOTUS: Border Wall Construction Can Resume, Saving Government a Half-Million Dollars a Day
sources.text:
The U.S. government had been suffering an unrecoverable loss of a half-million dollars a day until Monday, when the Supreme Court paused U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone’s order stopping construction of a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwest Texas.
On October 2, Judge Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from continuing construction on the border wall “until and unless” it satisfied the plaintiffs’ environmental and other objections.
Then, on October 14, Judge Cardone denied the government’s request to pause her ban until it could seek Supreme Court review of the matter.
As a result, DHS was forced to apply to the Supreme Court for a stay of the ban, which the High Court granted on Monday. The stay affords DHS time to file a writ of certiorari petitioning the High Court to take up the case.
The Supreme Court cited several reasons for granting the stay, including:
- The government “is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument” that Judge Cardone lacked the authority to halt the border wall’s construction.
- Cardone’s ruling “impedes the Government from advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity.”
- The government is suffering permanent harm from the half-million dollar daily costs being incurred by the delayed construction, since there is no way to recover those costs.
- Homeland Security’s interests outweigh any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by the plaintiffs.
- “The balance of the equities also favors the Government.”
In conclusion, the Supreme Court ruled that the construction ban is lifted until it either refuses to take up the case or takes it up and decides it:
“The injunction entered by the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas in case No. 3:26–cv–01099 is stayed pending the filing and disposition of the Government’s petition for a writ of certiorari, if such writ is timely sought. Should certiorari be denied, this stay shall terminate automatically. In the event certiorari is granted, the stay shall terminate upon the sending down of the judgment of this Court.”

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Hands Trump a Big Win on Border Wall
Supreme Court rules Trump Big Bend border wall construction can continue
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday ruled against Texans trying to stop the Trump administration from building a border wall system in the Big Bend region of Texas.
The unsigned ruling states that Justice Ketanji Jackson is the only justice who would deny the Trump administration’s application for a stay to reverse a lower court ruling.
At issue is a lawsuit filed in the Western District of Texas against the administration arguing waivers signed by Department of Homeland Security secretaries to bypass dozens of federal and state laws are unconstitutional.
Both DHS secretaries Kristi Noem and Markwayne Mullin invoked Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) when they signed waivers to bypass state and federal laws protecting the environment, air and water, historic landmarks, Indian burial grounds, endangered rivers, lands and species, The Center Square reported.
They argued the U.S. Customs and Border Protection Big Bend Sector “is an area of high illegal entry” despite CBP consistently reporting the lowest illegal crossings in the sector along the entire southwest border and in Texas. The sector spans more than 500 miles along the most rugged and remote terrain in Texas.
During the Biden administration, the Big Bend Sector reported the greatest number of illegal entries in its history but still among the lowest in the country, between half of one percent and two percent of all crossings, according to CBP data. Apprehensions in Big Bend National Park were less than half of one percent. Under the Trump administration, the lowest number of illegal entries were reported in U.S. history.
Several groups sued, including the Center for Biodiversity, arguing the DHS waivers violate the “Major Questions Doctrine,” which holds that federal agencies can’t legally implement major policy decisions unless authorized by Congress. The lawsuit also argues historically low Big Bend Sector illegal crossings don’t justify the reasons given for the waivers. The district court agreed, halting border wall construction, stating the Major Questions Doctrine needed to be answered.
Because the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals lacks jurisdiction in the case, the Trump administration filed an emergency petition with the Supreme Court. The administration argues the claims were baseless and the ruling was faulty.
The court issued a five-page unsigned ruling stating Section 201 of the IIRIRA grants the DHS secretary broad authority to construct border barriers and roads “to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.”
It also authorizes the secretary “‘to waive all legal requirements’” as “‘necessary to ensure expeditious construction’” of those barriers and roads “and sharply limits judicial review of all claims arising from such waiver determinations,” the court held. Specifically, the statute provides that “‘[a] cause of action or claim may only be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United States’” and courts “‘shall not have jurisdiction’” over nonconstitutional claims, the ruling states.
The Supreme Court criticized the major questions approach, saying, “Although styled as constitutional, that claim simply alleged that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority in issuing the waivers.
“We have long recognized that ‘claims simply alleging’ that the Executive Branch has exceeded its ‘statutory authority are not ‘constitutional’ claims,” the court said, adding that the district court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate the major questions doctrine claim.
It also said the IIRIRA allows the DHS secretary to issue waivers, stating, “Congress’s enactment of IIRIRA §102(c) – which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental protection and other conservation laws – reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert. … And courts ‘of equity cannot, in their discretion, reject the balance that Congress has struck in a statute.’”
The court reversed the lower court ruling, allowing construction to proceed as the case continues in federal court. The ruling is temporary until the case is settled in district court or the Supreme Court agrees to hear the case.
In response to the ruling, Laiken Jordahl with the Center for Biodiversity, said, the ruling “clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert, dynamite canyon walls and lock away a great American river from us all. And for what? All just to further enrich a few billionaire contractors while they permanently destroy Texas' crown-jewel national park. Because nobody else wants this.”
“The Trump administration and its contractors are hellbent on destroying one of America’s greatest national parks, and the Supreme Court just gave them the green light,” he said, noting that the litigation is ongoing. “This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”
Outgoing Republican U.S. Sen. John Cornyn also sided with plaintiffs, arguing, “A border wall is not the best solution for portions of this environment” and DHS should prioritize “smarter, more cost-effective security measures better suited to the area’s unique terrain.”

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday, Nov. 9, that President Donald Trump’s administration can resume construction of border barriers and related infrastructure in the Big Bend region of West Texas, overturning a federal court order that had halted the project over environmental and constitutional concerns.
In an unsigned 8-1 decision, the justices granted the administration’s emergency request to suspend an injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone in El Paso. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter and did not provide a written explanation.
The Supreme Court’s ruling in Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church allows construction to continue while litigation proceeds. The decision does not constitute a final ruling on the legality of the project.
The dispute concerns the Trump administration’s plans to expand border security infrastructure throughout the Big Bend Sector, which encompasses more than 500 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border, including Big Bend National Park.
The administration has proposed a combination of steel barriers, vehicle obstacles, patrol roads, surveillance cameras and detection equipment intended to deter illegal crossings and strengthen border enforcement.
“The Government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents,” the Supreme Court stated.
The justices emphasized that Congress had granted the Department of Homeland Security broad authority to expedite border barrier construction and waive certain legal requirements.
Under Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, the homeland security secretary may construct barriers and roads in areas experiencing high levels of illegal entry.
The statute also authorizes the secretary to waive legal requirements considered necessary to accelerate construction, while sharply limiting judicial review of those decisions.
The Supreme Court concluded that Congress had expressed a clear preference for expedited border construction when the federal government invokes those authorities.
The ruling followed an October injunction in which Cardone ordered the government to stop construction and ground-disturbing activities throughout the Big Bend Sector.
The judge questioned whether the administration possessed sufficient congressional authority to waive environmental and conservation laws for construction in an area with comparatively low levels of illegal border crossings.
According to The Texas Tribune’s Nov. 9 report, the judge’s order applied to work within Big Bend National Park and surrounding federal, state and private land.
The Trump administration appealed, arguing that the injunction interfered with the government’s ability to enforce immigration laws and protect the southern border.
Federal attorneys maintained that the district court exceeded its authority because Congress had specifically restricted lawsuits challenging border construction waivers.
The Supreme Court agreed that the government’s interest in border security outweighed the harms identified by the plaintiffs at this stage of the litigation.
The decision represents a significant legal development for Trump’s broader effort to expand physical barriers along the southern border.
Congress approved approximately $46 billion for border construction during the summer, providing funding for expanded barriers, roads and surveillance infrastructure.
According to The Associated Press, Customs and Border Protection has been constructing approximately 12 miles of barriers per week along portions of the border.
The Big Bend project has become particularly controversial because of the region’s remote terrain, environmental protections and relatively low historical rates of illegal crossings.
Located along the Rio Grande, Big Bend National Park contains extensive desert landscapes, mountains, canyons and habitats supporting a wide range of wildlife.
The administration’s plans include 30-foot steel barriers in some areas of the broader sector, along with vehicle barriers and new roads.
Customs and Border Protection has indicated that it does not plan to construct a 30-foot pedestrian wall inside Big Bend National Park itself. Instead, the proposed work within the park includes vehicle barriers, patrol roads and other security infrastructure.
The distinction is significant because the project encompasses multiple types of construction across a large geographic area rather than a continuous steel wall through the national park.
The administration has argued that illegal crossings, drug trafficking and other criminal activity justify additional border security measures.
Federal officials also contend that gaps in border infrastructure could encourage unauthorized crossings to shift toward the Big Bend region as barriers are completed elsewhere.
Opponents dispute the necessity of extensive construction in an area historically recording some of the lowest migrant apprehension rates along the southern border.
The lawsuit was brought by environmental organizations and local residents who argued that the administration improperly bypassed legal protections governing public lands, historic sites and wildlife habitats.
According to Reuters’ coverage of the decision, the challengers include the Center for Biological Diversity and other plaintiffs seeking to prevent damage to the region’s natural and cultural resources.
Their objections focus on the potential destruction of wildlife habitat, damage to sensitive desert landscapes and disruptions to tourism and local businesses.
Some residents and conservation advocates have argued that surveillance technology, including drones and remote sensors, could address security concerns without extensive physical construction.
The project has also encountered opposition from Republicans.
Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, has raised concerns about the proposed infrastructure in the Big Bend region, illustrating that disagreement over the project extends beyond traditional partisan divisions.
Supporters of the administration’s approach argue that federal authorities should retain flexibility to deploy physical barriers and surveillance systems where they determine additional security is necessary.
The disagreement centers partly on whether the Department of Homeland Security can invoke broad statutory waiver powers in areas where the need for extensive construction is contested.
The Supreme Court’s ruling addressed that procedural and legal dispute rather than making a final determination about the environmental consequences of construction.
In its opinion, the court noted that the challengers argued the project would diminish their ability to use and enjoy the Big Bend region.
However, the justices concluded that Congress had authorized expedited construction despite potential environmental and recreational consequences.
The court also emphasized that existing federal law restricts challenges to waiver decisions, permitting claims alleging constitutional violations while excluding many other legal challenges.
The decision temporarily restores the government’s ability to proceed while the administration seeks further Supreme Court review or the case continues in federal court.
Jackson’s dissent indicates disagreement with granting emergency relief, although she did not explain her reasoning.
No other justice publicly dissented.
The ruling leaves several questions unresolved, including the ultimate scope of the administration’s waiver authority and whether the challengers can succeed on their remaining constitutional arguments.
The federal government must also determine how quickly work can resume in areas affected by the injunction.
Construction crews had previously begun excavating and clearing portions of the project area before the district court ordered work to stop.
The Supreme Court’s decision removes that immediate restriction, allowing federal officials and contractors to restart activities authorized under the government’s construction plans.
The litigation remains active, and future court proceedings could affect the project’s final scope.
For now, the ruling gives Trump an important legal victory on one of his administration’s central immigration priorities, clearing the way for additional border security construction across the Big Bend region while the broader constitutional dispute continues.

sources.text:
The Supreme Court on Nov. 9 paused a preliminary injunction that had blocked the Trump administration’s border barrier construction in an area including Big Bend National Park in Texas, allowing work to resume while the litigation plays out.
In an Oct. 2 order, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone sided with an environmental group and others who claimed that the project was unconstitutional, breached the separation of powers, and took land from residents.
“This case involves a baseless injunction that halts a major portion of the construction of the border wall,” U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the emergency application. “Moreover, leaving a 300-plus-mile gap in border defenses would act as a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors to exploit as other routes close off.”
The Trump administration argued that continuing construction was crucial because the Big Bend region encompasses nearly one-quarter of the U.S.–Mexico border.
In its new ruling, the nation’s highest court stated that Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 gives the homeland security secretary broad authority to build border barriers and roads “to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.”
The same section also authorizes the secretary “to waive all legal requirements” as “necessary to ensure expeditious construction” of those barriers and roads and “sharply limits judicial review of all claims arising from such waiver determinations.”
The act states that “‘[a] cause of action or claim may only be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United States’” and that courts “shall not have jurisdiction” over claims not alleging a constitutional violation, the court stated.
Earlier this year, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin invoked Section 102’s waiver authority to initiate a border-construction project at the U.S.–Mexico border, in a region that Customs and Border Protection calls the “Big Bend Sector.”
The secretary found that the sector “is an area of high illegal entry” that needs additional border barriers and waived a variety of environmental and conservation laws to allow construction to proceed, the court stated.
The justices reasoned that the environmental lawsuit was really about whether Mullin exceeded the authority Congress gave him, not about whether he violated the Constitution. Dressing up a statutory complaint as a constitutional one falls outside what the statute allows, they said.
The plaintiffs had argued that the waivers violated the major questions doctrine under the Constitution. That doctrine states that Congress must speak clearly when it hands an agency power over an issue of vast economic or political significance, rather than letting the agency infer that authority from vague language.
The district court agreed that this counted as a constitutional claim because it viewed the doctrine as a clear statement rule grounded in the separation of powers. The separation of powers is a constitutional doctrine that divides the government into three distinct and independent branches to prevent the concentration of power.
The Supreme Court disagreed. It stated that the doctrine is a tool courts use when interpreting statutes, not a free-standing constitutional claim.
“There is no such thing as a ‘constitutional’ major-questions claim,” the court stated in its written opinion.
The Supreme Court also stated that the remaining factors for a stay favored the government. The injunction delays construction and is costing almost half a million dollars per day in expenses that “cannot be recouped.”
Weighing the two sides, the justices noted that Congress, by giving the secretary waiver authority, had already chosen expeditious border construction over the environmental and recreational harms the plaintiffs alleged.

The District Court acknowledged that its jurisdiction was limited to constitutional claims. But it nonetheless concluded that respondents' "major questions doctrine claim" qualified because, in its view, the "major questions doctrine is a constitutional clear statement rule grounded in separation of powers." The court further held that respondents' "major questions doctrine claim" was likely to succeed on the merits because the Secretary lacked "'clear congressional authorization' to issue" the waivers. Because the Fifth Circuit lacks jurisdiction to hear this case, IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(C), the Solicitor General filed an application requesting either summary reversal or a stay of the District Court's preliminary injunction.
We grant the requested stay. The Government is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument that the District Court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate respondents' so-called major-questions-doctrine claim. However it is labeled, respondents' claim does not "'alleg[e] a violation of the Constitution of the United States,'" the only type of claim the statute permits district courts to adjudicate. IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(A). It alleges instead that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority. And we have long recognized that "claims simply alleging" that the Executive Branch has exceeded its "statutory authority are not 'constitutional' claims." Dalton v. Specter (1994).
That conclusion does not change where, as here, a plaintiff invokes the major-questions doctrine. Many canons and rules of statutory interpretation reflect constitutional principles, including "constitutional avoidance, the clear-statement federalism rules, and the presumption against retroactivity." When courts invoke those canons, however, they do so in service of adjudicating statutory claims, not constitutional ones. The same is true when a court invokes "the major questions canon of statutory interpretation." There is no such thing as a "constitutional" major-questions claim….
Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area. But Congress's enactment of IIRIRA §102(c)—which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws—reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert. And courts "of equity cannot, in their discretion, reject the balance that Congress has struck in a statute." The Government's interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents….

Liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only member of the court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, to publicly dissent from the decision.
The lawsuit was brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend-area river guide and a group seeking to preserve a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas, that says its fragile adobe structure is threatened by the border construction.

The waivers were issued under a 1996 federal law aimed at facilitating the construction of barriers in areas of high illegal crossings at the southern border.
In Monday's ruling, the Supreme Court said the law at issue likely precludes judicial review of the claims brought in the lawsuit.
'HIGH ILLEGAL ENTRY'
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and his predecessor Kristi Noem, Trump appointees who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an "area of high illegal entry," requiring additional barriers to control the border.
The administration also said that border officials have seized massive quantities of drugs in the region and that cartels operate south of the region in Mexico.
The administration said that most of the construction in the Big Bend sector, spanning more than 300 miles (480 km), will take place on privately owned land. Big Bend National Park would get a 17-mile (27-km) noncontiguous vehicle barrier system but not the kind of 30-foot (9-meter) pedestrian barrier that is slated for other areas, according to the administration.
In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its potential impact on the park's landscape and wildlife. Crews had begun clearing land in the park for roads and border security infrastructure, prompting protests and lawsuits seeking to halt the work.
'ECOLOGICALLY AND CULTURALLY SIGNIFICANT'
Absent the waivers, the project would have to comply with numerous laws including the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act to alter the landscape in "one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States," according to the challengers.

sources.text:
The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume construction on a major border barrier project in Texas' remote Big Bend region, with liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissenting.
The high court granted the administration’s request to stay a lower-court preliminary injunction that had blocked Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin from using federal waiver authority to advance the project.
Jackson was the sole justice identified in the order as opposing the action. The decision stated simply: “JUSTICE JACKSON would deny the application for stay.” Jackson did not provide a written explanation.
Read More on News
The majority found that the administration was “exceedingly likely to prevail” on its argument that the lower court lacked jurisdiction to consider the challengers' claims.
The ruling provides an immediate legal boost to the administration’s plans to expand barriers across the U.S.-Mexico border, a project that has drawn opposition from conservationists and local groups over potential landscape and ecological damage.
President Donald Trump has made reducing illegal crossings of the southern border one of the main policy priorities of his presidency. His "One Big Beautiful Bill," which was signed into law last year, earmarked $46.5 billion for the construction of fencing and other obstacles to deter illegal immigration across the 1,954-mile-long border.
Planned barriers include hundreds of miles of 30-foot border wall along with surveillance systems and river barriers. This will require building on private as well as federally owned land, where initial construction of the border wall was concentrated.
In August, bulldozers were seen at the Big Bend National Park clearing land ahead of construction, sparking cross-party anger. In response, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) halted the work, but the pause ended on September 30.
The Legal Battle
The lawsuit was brought by an individual river guide, the environmental nonprofit Center for Biological Diversity, and Friends of the Ruidosa Church, an organization dedicated to preserving a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas.
The challengers argued that Mullin exceeded congressional authority by using a federal waiver provision to set aside environmental and conservation laws. They invoked the “major-questions doctrine,” arguing that such a consequential exercise of executive power required clear authorization from Congress.
The administration countered that Congress explicitly gave the DHS secretary broad authority to waive legal requirements to expedite border barriers. In its filing, the government called the lower court order a “baseless injunction that halts a major portion of the construction of the border wall.”
What the Supreme Court Decided
At the center of the dispute is Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA) of 1996, which grants the DHS secretary broad authority to construct barriers and roads and “to waive all legal requirements” considered “necessary to ensure expeditious construction.”
On October 2, the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas issued a preliminary injunction blocking the waivers, concluding that Mullin lacked “clear congressional authorization.”
After the injunction, a spokesperson for U.S. Customs and Border Protection told Newsweek: "We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region. We are working with the Department of Justice on next steps."
The Supreme Court focused on whether the lower court had jurisdiction to review the matter. Under the statute, courts can review challenges alleging violations of the U.S. Constitution, but they lack jurisdiction over nonconstitutional claims. The majority wrote that "there is no such thing as a ‘constitutional’ major-questions claim."
The court's majority also found that continuing to block construction would cause irreparable harm to the government. According to a CBP declaration, the injunction was costing nearly $500,000 per day—money that “cannot be recouped”—while preventing the government from advancing its “compelling interests” in “border security and integrity.”
While acknowledging concerns regarding aesthetic, recreational, and environmental damage, the court concluded that Congress had already struck a balance in favor of expedited border construction.
What Happens Next
The order removes the injunction while the government petitions the court to formally hear the case. If the court denies the petition, the stay will automatically end; if the justices agree to hear the case, the stay will remain in place until a final judgment is issued.
For now, the ruling gives the administration the legal opening it sought to continue its Big Bend border construction efforts as the broader legal battle proceeds.

sources.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court agreed on Monday to end a lower court blockade that sought to stop President Trump’s border wall construction along the U.S.-Mexico border. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson would have allowed the blockade to remain in place.
In its per curiam ruling, the high court granted an emergency application by the Trump administration to temporarily pause an Oct. 2 ruling by District Judge Kathleen Cardone. The Bush 43 appointee issued a preliminary injunction preventing the government from constructing border wall in the Big Bend region of Southwest Texas.
The case deals with a series of waivers that former and current Department of Homeland Security Secretaries Kristi Noem and Markwayne Mullin signed to set aside various conservation and environmental laws that blocked the wall in the Big Bend area, which includes the region’s national park. According to U.S. Solicitor General John Sauer, the secretaries made the decision in accordance with federal immigration law after determining that the Big Bend region “is an area of high illegal entry” that required construction.
Cardone argued in an Oct. 14 opinion explaining her injunction that the challengers are likely to prevail on their claims that the DHS secretaries lacked the legal authority to waive the contested laws under the major questions doctrine. That doctrine states that executive agencies cannot make regulatory decisions on issues of “vast ‘economic and political significance’” unless Congress specifically says so.
Sauer argued in the administration’s SCOTUS application that Congress “denied district courts jurisdiction to entertain” claims like those made in the case. The solicitor general further contended that challengers’ “major-questions claim borders on frivolous” and that Cardone “effectively rewrote [the law in question] to atextually limit the Secretary’s waiver authority to only areas of ‘comparative[ly]’ high illegal entry.”
In its Monday ruling, the Supreme Court found that the administration is “exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument” that Cardone did not have jurisdiction to adjudicate the challengers’ “so-called major-questions-doctrine claim.” The majority held that, regardless of how “it is labeled, respondents’ claim does not ‘“alleg[e] a violation of the Constitution of the United States,”’ the only type of claim the statute permits district courts to adjudicate.”
“It alleges instead that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority. And we have long recognized that ‘claims simply alleging’ that the Executive Branch has exceeded its ‘statutory authority are not “constitutional” claims,’” the decision reads. “That conclusion does not change where, as here, a plaintiff invokes the major-questions doctrine.”
The high court went on to note that the other factors used to determine whether a stay is warranted also favor the government. This includes the administration’s demonstration that it will suffer irreparable harm if Cardone’s injunction is permitted to remain in place, as well as a showing that the “balance of the equities” tilts in its favor.
“Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area. But Congress’s enactment of [the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act] — which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws — reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert,” the court ruled. “And courts ‘of equity cannot, in their discretion, reject the balance that Congress has struck in a statute.’ … The Government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents.”
Justice Jackson did not provide a reason for her dissent.
According to Monday’s ruling, Cardone’s injunction “is stayed pending the filing and disposition of the Government’s petition for a writ of certiorari, if such writ is timely sought.” The Supreme Court’s pause will terminate if a petition to SCOTUS is denied by the high court or if SCOTUS agrees to consider the matter and issue a judgment on the merits of the case.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court cleared the way Monday for the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, a blow to bipartisan opponents who had argued the project is a waste of money that threatens the unique landscape.
The border wall is a signature project of President Donald Trump, who has long vowed to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.
Landowners and business owners in the Big Bend region, environmentalists and others who’ve opposed the construction project were bitterly disappointed with the court’s decision.
“This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the groups that sued to stop the construction. “They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”
Republicans in Congress last summer funded the project with $46 billion, and Customs and Border Protection has been rapidly erecting 12 miles of barriers a week across the entire border with a goal of eventually covering the entire 2,000-mile border with a mixture of 30-foot-tall steel walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology designed to stop illegal immigration and smuggling.
The government has pushed forward by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass regulations. Those rules are aimed at protecting the environment, but have historically slowed down major construction projects.
Big Bend residents of both parties oppose the project
In Texas’s Big Bend region, bipartisan opposition has rallied to fight back against the project, which would include 30-foot-tall steel walls in some areas as well as vehicle barriers and new roads.
They’ve argued that the barriers are a waste of money that threaten the local economy and lifestyle in an area of historically low illegal immigration. They say the job could be better done using only surveillance technology like drones.
A judge in Texas sided with opponents, finding that Congress likely had not clearly authorized such broad waivers for an area with the southern border’s lowest rate of migrant apprehensions. She ordered an immediate stop to all construction-related activity in the area, which includes Big Bend National Park as well as land up and down river in state and private hands.
The Trump administration filed an emergency appeal, saying there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in Big Bend. More traffic could also be funneled there if there’s a gap in the wall, federal attorneys argued.
Customs and Border Protection head Rodney Scott said in an interview with The Associated Press that if the Big Bend area were left without a wall or other border infrastructure while other areas along the border get those fortifications, he’s convinced it would be swiftly overrun by cartels.
The Supreme Court agreed that the law sharply limits judges’ powers to intervene when the federal government decides speedy border barrier construction is necessary. The majority paused the lower court decision as the case plays out. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
CBP did not immediately respond to questions about how swiftly construction could restart. The agency started building an initial section of border wall in one area of the roughly 500-mile stretch that makes up the Big Bend region, but that was stopped with the judge’s order.
Construction activity in national park sparked outrage
The agency has encountered intense opposition from landowners up and down the region when it comes to getting permissions to enter their land to survey and build.
The Center for Biological Diversity sued over the construction, along with Friends of the Ruidosa Church and a river guide in the Big Bend area. Jordahl said it was the first time the government had waived a broad set of environmental laws inside a national park.
David Keller lives in the Big Bend region, is a member of the board of Conserve Big Bend and is a plaintiff in a separate lawsuit of landowners opposing the border wall projects.
He called the court’s decision devastating: “Everything is on the line again.”
Keller called the border infrastructure projects the “industrialization of one of the last best open undeveloped wild places in the lower 48 states.”
“We can’t afford to lose any more. Not an ounce. Not an acre,” he said. “We need wild country to be who we are, to be fully human, to be American I would say.”
The projects have drawn criticism from both Democrats and Republicans, including outgoing Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, who wrote an op-ed arguing against the project published Monday in the San Antonio Express-News hours before the court’s decision.
“A combination of modern technology, adequate staffing, and meaningful cooperation with local officials and landowners offers a more sensible and effective path forward than indiscriminate construction of unnecessary barriers,” Cornyn wrote.
The government in August paused construction activity in Big Bend National Park that sparked outrage when bulldozers were spotted breaking ground in the park.
The government has repeatedly said no steel walls are planned for the national park. Initial plans included a new road as well as some vehicle barriers in the park. CBP has said in court filings that it will come forward with a finalized plan for what it intends to build in the national park but so far hasn’t done so while the case was at the Supreme Court.

sources.text:
The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. In a four-page, unsigned opinion, the justices granted the government’s request to pause an order by a federal district judge that had temporarily halted the project. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would have denied the government’s request.
The dispute began earlier this year, when then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws to authorize construction of the wall in the Big Bend region, which includes parts of Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the DHS secretary the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. When they announced the waivers, Noem and Mullin indicated that the Big Bend area “is an area of high illegal entry” requiring additional walls and barriers.
A group of plaintiffs opposed to the construction – an environmental group, a local landowner who works as a river guide, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Big Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.
In a written opinion that she released on Oct. 14, Cardone reasoned that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that the DHS secretary did not have the authority to issue the waivers. She relied on the major questions doctrine – the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so very clearly. In particular, she emphasized, the Big Bend region is not an area with a high number of illegal entries. To the contrary, she stated, although it “comprises over 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border,” it makes up only a tiny percentage (“between 0.3% and 2.2%”) of the migrants apprehended while crossing the border. Therefore, she wrote, “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border. If that were the case, Congress could have simply authorized construction ‘to deter illegal crossings.’” The major questions doctrine instructs courts to avoid “interpretations that would render limiting language meaningless,” Cardone concluded.
After Cardone declined to pause her ruling to give the government time to seek Supreme Court review, the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court, where it asked the justices not only to temporarily freeze Cardone’s order but also to grant review and summarily (that is, without additional briefing or oral argument) reverse it. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that Cardone lacked the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because their complaint specifically alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to issue the waivers” under the IIRIRA – which, he said, was a statutory claim that “Congress denied district courts” the authority “to entertain.” But in any event, Sauer continued, even if the DHS secretary’s power to issue waivers under IIRIRA “implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”
The challengers urged the justices to leave Cardone’s order in place. Eric Glitzenstein, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the justices in a 40-page filing that if her order were paused or lifted, it would permit the Trump administration to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”
The challengers argued that the major questions doctrine applied to their claim. They emphasized that the DHS secretary’s “decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure, even through national and state parks where border crossings are miniscule, is a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.” Because Congress “did not clearly authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here,” they wrote, the government’s “actions therefore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine.”
In Monday’s opinion, the justices denied the government’s request to summarily reverse Cardone’s ruling but granted its request to put it on hold. “The Government,” the court explained, “is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument” that Cardone did not have the power to consider the challengers’ “so-called major-questions-doctrine claim.” That claim, the court emphasized, contends only “that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority,” which is not a constitutional claim. This is true, the court continued, even if the challengers rely on the major-questions doctrine, because that doctrine is a rule used to interpret laws. “There is no such thing as a ‘constitutional’ major-questions claim.”
The other factors that courts normally consider in deciding whether to pause a lower court’s decision also point in the government’s favor, the justices said. For example, Cardone’s order “delays the Government’s construction of border barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector” and, as a result, “impedes the Government from advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity.” Moreover, the government is suffering permanent harm from the costs – “nearly half a million dollars … per day” – that it is incurring while the construction is on hold, but which cannot be recovered. Finally, the court wrote, “[t]he Government’s interest … outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by” the challengers.

By REBECCA SANTANA and LINDSAY WHITEHURST
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court cleared the way Monday for the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, a blow to bipartisan opponents who had argued the project is a waste of money that threatens the unique landscape.
The border wall is a signature project of President Donald Trump, who has long vowed to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.
Landowners and business owners in the Big Bend region, environmentalists and others who’ve opposed the construction project were bitterly disappointed with the court’s decision.
“This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the groups that sued to stop the construction. “They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”
Republicans in Congress last summer funded the project with $46 billion, and Customs and Border Protection has been rapidly erecting 12 miles of barriers a week across the entire border with a goal of eventually covering the entire 2,000-mile border with a mixture of 30-foot-tall steel walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology designed to stop illegal immigration and smuggling.
The government has pushed forward by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass regulations. Those rules are aimed at protecting the environment, but have historically slowed down major construction projects.
Big Bend residents of both parties oppose the project
In Texas’s Big Bend region, bipartisan opposition has rallied to fight back against the project, which would include 30-foot-tall steel walls in some areas as well as vehicle barriers and new roads.
They’ve argued that the barriers are a waste of money that threaten the local economy and lifestyle in an area of historically low illegal immigration. They say the job could be better done using only surveillance technology like drones.
A judge in Texas sided with opponents, finding that Congress likely had not clearly authorized such broad waivers for an area with the southern border’s lowest rate of migrant apprehensions. She ordered an immediate stop to all construction-related activity in the area, which includes Big Bend National Park as well as land up and down river in state and private hands.
The Trump administration filed an emergency appeal, saying there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in Big Bend. More traffic could also be funneled there if there’s a gap in the wall, federal attorneys argued.
Customs and Border Protection head Rodney Scott said in an interview with The Associated Press that if the Big Bend area were left without a wall or other border infrastructure while other areas along the border get those fortifications, he’s convinced it would be swiftly overrun by cartels.
The Supreme Court agreed that the law sharply limits judges’ powers to intervene when the federal government decides speedy border barrier construction is necessary. The majority paused the lower court decision as the case plays out. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
CBP did not immediately respond to questions about how swiftly construction could restart. The agency started building an initial section of border wall in one area of the roughly 500-mile stretch that makes up the Big Bend region, but that was stopped with the judge’s order.
Construction activity in national park sparked outrage
The agency has encountered intense opposition from landowners up and down the region when it comes to getting permissions to enter their land to survey and build.
The Center for Biological Diversity sued over the construction, along with Friends of the Ruidosa Church and a river guide in the Big Bend area. Jordahl said it was the first time the government had waived a broad set of environmental laws inside a national park.
David Keller lives in the Big Bend region, is a member of the board of Conserve Big Bend and is a plaintiff in a separate lawsuit of landowners opposing the border wall projects.
He called the court’s decision devastating: “Everything is on the line again.”
Keller called the border infrastructure projects the “industrialization of one of the last best open undeveloped wild places in the lower 48 states.”
“We can’t afford to lose any more. Not an ounce. Not an acre,” he said. “We need wild country to be who we are, to be fully human, to be American I would say.”
The projects have drawn criticism from both Democrats and Republicans, including outgoing Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, who wrote an op-ed arguing against the project published Monday in the San Antonio Express-News hours before the court’s decision.
“A combination of modern technology, adequate staffing, and meaningful cooperation with local officials and landowners offers a more sensible and effective path forward than indiscriminate construction of unnecessary barriers,” Cornyn wrote.
The government in August paused construction activity in Big Bend National Park that sparked outrage when bulldozers were spotted breaking ground in the park.
The government has repeatedly said no steel walls are planned for the national park. Initial plans included a new road as well as some vehicle barriers in the park. CBP has said in court filings that it will come forward with a finalized plan for what it intends to build in the national park but so far hasn’t done so while the case was at the Supreme Court.

sources.text:
Sometimes, what you call something matters. Other times, the courts aren't particularly interested in your creative labeling.
The Supreme Court made that second point abundantly clear Monday, handing the Trump administration a win in its effort to resume border wall construction in Texas — and delivering a rather pointed lesson about the difference between constitutional claims and statutory ones.
In Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church, the High Court granted the administration's request to stay an October 2 preliminary injunction issued by a federal district judge in the Western District of Texas. That injunction had halted construction of border barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector along the U.S.-Mexico border.
At issue is a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA), which gives the Homeland Security secretary broad authority to construct border barriers and waive legal requirements that might impede their construction — including environmental and conservation laws.
There's a catch for anyone wishing to challenge those waivers in court, though: Congress specifically limited judicial review to claims alleging violations of the Constitution.
Enter the plaintiffs, including a river guide, an environmental organization, and a group dedicated to preserving a historic Texas church. They challenged the administration's waivers using what's known as the major questions doctrine.
That's a legal principle requiring clear congressional authorization before federal agencies can exercise certain powers of vast economic or political significance. The plaintiffs argued that the administration lacked that authorization. And the district court agreed, concluding that the major questions doctrine is rooted in constitutional separation-of-powers principles and therefore provided a constitutional basis for the challenge.
SCOTUS delivered a big NOPE to that view, however. In an unsigned, five-page opinion, the justices explained that while the major questions doctrine certainly reflects constitutional concerns, it's still a tool courts use to interpret statutes.
And the Court didn't mince words:
There is no such thing as a “constitutional” major-questions claim.
In other words, arguing that an agency exceeded the authority Congress granted it doesn't magically become a constitutional claim simply because the underlying legal principle has constitutional roots.
Call it what you like. It's still a statutory challenge.
Moreover, Congress expressly barred the lower courts from entertaining those challenges to the secretary's waiver decisions. Thus, the Court concluded that the administration was exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument that the district court lacked jurisdiction.
The justices also noted that the injunction was costing the government nearly $500,000 per day in unrecoverable expenses, according to a Customs and Border Protection official, and interfering with Congress's expressly stated preference for expedited border construction.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson would have denied the stay, though she offered no written explanation.
Now, there's a caveat here: Monday's order is not a final decision resolving the underlying lawsuit. What today's order means is that the injunction remains suspended while the administration pursues Supreme Court review.
But the ruling carries significance well beyond this particular stretch of border wall.
Congress can limit lower federal courts' authority to hear certain disputes. And when it does, litigants cannot sidestep those limits simply by giving their statutory arguments a constitutional makeover. (A rose by any other name...)
It's also important to bear in mind that the separation of powers works in more than one direction. And sometimes, the most consequential question isn't whether the government acted lawfully, but whether the court had the authority to decide that question in the first place.

The order pauses the injunction while the government seeks Supreme Court review. It does not resolve the entire lawsuit.

For Immediate Release, November 9, 2026

Supreme Court Clears Way for Border Wall Construction Across Big Bend
WASHINGTON— The U.S. Supreme Court today lifted a federal court order that halted border barrier and road construction across the Big Bend region of Texas for the past month, allowing the Trump administration to resume construction in Big Bend National Park and along more than 500 miles of the Rio Grande. The administration could also begin construction in Big Bend Ranch State Park.
The Supreme Court ruling suspends the district court’s injunction while the lawsuit proceeds. It is not a final ruling on the legality of the sweeping waiver of environmental laws.
“The Trump administration and its contractors are hellbent on destroying one of America’s greatest national parks, and the Supreme Court just gave them the green light,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity. “This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”
The injunction, issued Oct. 2 by U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone, was sought by the Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church and a Big Bend-area river guide and landowner. Their lawsuit challenges the federal government’s waiver of dozens of laws to fast-track border barrier construction through Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park and across the Big Bend region. The suit says the waivers violate the major questions doctrine, which requires explicit congressional approval for actions with vast economic and political consequences.
The waivers marked the first time in U.S. history that the federal government swept aside a broad slate of environmental laws — including the Endangered Species Act, National Wild and Scenic Rivers Act and National Park Service Organic Act — inside a national park.
Bulldozers started tearing into Big Bend National Park near the iconic Santa Elena Canyon on Aug. 6 and were documented plowing new routes for vehicle barriers into both the east and west sides of Mariscal Mountain. Contractors have stockpiled heavy equipment across the Big Bend region, where staging yards have been cleared, worker camps built and water wells drilled.
On Aug. 17, responding to widespread nonpartisan outrage, Customs and Border Protection announced a pause in construction activities. That pause lapsed Sept. 30 and without a preliminary injunction or action from Congress, work could have resumed at any moment.
“The destruction we’ve already seen in Big Bend unleashed a firestorm of outrage so severe that the administration was forced to pause its plans,” said Jordahl. “If the bulldozers return now, public opposition will only grow. Americans care deeply about this extraordinary national park and they won’t stand by quietly if its irreplaceable landscapes are butchered and paved over. The damage done to Big Bend will be felt for future generations of Texans and Americans, and this administration will bear responsibility for the natural heritage we lose.”
According to Customs and Border Protection’s online map, the agency plans to build vehicle barriers and patrol roads across Big Bend National Park, including in rugged and remote areas such as Mariscal Mountain that would require extensive dynamite blasting. The plans also include building in remote walled canyons where no unauthorized vehicle crossings have been documented and where vehicles cannot access the border with Mexico.
More than 140 outfitters, local businesses and recreation groups have urged Texas leaders to protect public access to the Rio Grande and halt the project. They warned that closing river access and building permanent barriers and roads through the canyon corridor would put river outfitters out of business and devastate the regional economy.
Texas Sen. John Cornyn voiced his opposition to border wall construction through Big Bend in an op-ed published today in the San Antonio Express-News.
The Big Bend Sector covers 517 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border, amounting to more than a quarter of the border’s total length. The region saw just 1.3% of total border apprehensions in 2025. Within Big Bend National Park, apprehensions accounted for 0.045% of the national total. For decades the National Park Service and Customs and Border Protection have conducted border enforcement while preserving the park’s irreplaceable natural heritage and recreational opportunities.
The plaintiffs are represented by attorneys at the Center for Biological Diversity and Texas Civil Rights Project.
The Center for Biological Diversity is a national, nonprofit conservation organization with more than 1.8 million members and online activists dedicated to the protection of endangered species and wild places.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a Joe Biden appointee, was the only noted dissent.
Big Bend’s harsh desert environment and rugged mountain ranges have doubled as a natural barrier to travel. The region includes national and state parks, ranchlands, and unique historic and cultural resources.

“Leaving a 300-plus-mile gap in border defenses would act as a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors to exploit as other routes close off,” the government wrote.
